html:
Retirement often brings accumulated gold - jewellery, coins, and biscuits held for decades - and the question of whether to sell. For many retirees, gold represents a significant portion of their wealth.

This guide covers the tax angle (often more favourable in retirement), the practical selling process, and key considerations specific to retirees.

At a Glance

Gold held 24+ months?

Almost certainly yes for retirees - 12.5% LTCG applies

Retirement income tax benefit?

Yes - lower total income may push you to 0% or 5% slab

Senior citizen LTCG exemption?

Basic exemption ₹3L (instead of ₹2.5L) - but LTCG is flat 12.5%

TDS on gold sale?

No TDS on gold sale - but capital gain must be declared in ITR

PAN required?

Yes if sale > ₹2,00,000

Last Updated

May 2026

Tax on Selling Gold in Retirement

For most retirees selling gold held for 24+ months:
• Capital gains tax: 12.5% LTCG on the profit (sale price minus original purchase price)
• This is a flat rate regardless of your total income - LTCG is not added to income and taxed at slab rate

However, your basic exemption (₹3 lakh for senior citizens 60+, ₹5 lakh for super senior citizens 80+) offsets other income first. If your total taxable income is low, LTCG may be partially offset by the remaining basic exemption.

Important: If you have held the gold for decades but cannot prove the original purchase price, use the fair market value on 1 April 2001 as the cost basis. For very old ancestral gold, a chartered accountant can help establish this.

When to Sell in Retirement

  • Medical expenses - gold is often the fastest way to raise cash; same-day payment is possible
  • Property purchase or renovation - gold provides liquidity without fixed deposit penalties
  • Helping children with education or marriage - common use of accumulated gold
  • Simplifying your estate - reducing physical gold reduces the complexity of inheritance for your family
  • If gold is your only liquid asset and you need regular income - a Gold ETF or SGB might be a better ongoing form after selling physical gold

Practical Process for Retirees

  1. Gather the gold pieces you plan to sell - jewellery, coins and biscuits are all accepted
  2. Check the hallmark on each piece (916 for 22K, 750 for 18K) to understand the approximate value before visiting
  3. Bring Aadhaar card - mandatory for all gold sales
  4. Bring PAN card if the total sale exceeds ₹2,00,000 (very likely for significant holdings)
  5. Keep the sale receipt for your ITR - declare the capital gain in the financial year of the sale
  6. If TDS is deducted by any party: it will appear in Form 26AS and can be claimed as credit in ITR

Estate Planning Consideration

If you hold significant gold and are thinking about estate planning:
• Selling gold and distributing proceeds is simpler than leaving physical gold to multiple heirs
• Physical gold in a locker requires all nominees/heirs to coordinate for access after your passing
• Document every piece of gold you own: weight, purity, purchase price, location
• Keep sale receipts for pieces already sold - heirs may need this for tax purposes

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I pay tax on selling gold after retirement?

Yes - capital gains tax applies. For gold held 24+ months, LTCG at 12.5% is due on the profit. This is regardless of whether you are retired.

Is there a senior citizen exemption on gold LTCG?

Senior citizens (60+) have a higher basic exemption of ₹3L. LTCG itself is a flat 12.5% rate. The basic exemption applies to other income first; any remaining can offset LTCG in limited cases - consult your CA.

What is the cost basis for gold bought decades ago?

If the purchase price is unknown, use the fair market value (IBJA rate) on 1 April 2001 as the cost basis. A chartered accountant can help calculate this.

Can I sell gold without income tax hassle after retirement?

The selling process is straightforward - 20–35 minutes at the branch. The tax calculation happens at ITR time (usually July–September). Keep the sale receipt.

Is selling gold the right move in retirement?

Depends on your financial need. Gold is a good emergency or opportunity fund. If you do not need the money, continuing to hold is also fine.

Can my son or daughter sell gold on my behalf?

Yes - they can sell on your behalf with their own Aadhaar (the receipt will be in their name). Ensure you both understand the tax reporting implication.

What if I lose the original gold purchase receipt?

No purchase receipt is needed to sell the gold. However, you will need to estimate the cost basis for capital gains tax calculation - use IBJA rates from the approximate purchase period or 1 April 2001 FMV.

Selling gold to fund a house down payment is one of the most common and practical reasons people sell gold in India. Gold is among the most liquid assets a family can hold, and converting it to property is a well-understood strategy across generations.

This guide tells you how much gold you need for common down payment amounts, the selling process, and the key tax consideration.

Selling Process: From Gold to Bank Account in One Day

  1. XRF purity testing and weighing - 15–20 minutes
  2. Payment by bank transfer (mandatory for amounts above ₹2,00,000 under Section 269ST)
  3. Funds appear in your account within 2–4 hours or same working day via NEFT/IMPS
  4. Use the proceeds for your property down payment or booking amount

Tax: Selling Gold to Buy Property

Selling gold triggers capital gains tax regardless of how you use the money:
• Gold held 24+ months → 12.5% LTCG on the profit
• No special exemption for using gold proceeds to buy a home (unlike property capital gains, which have Section 54 exemptions)

Note: Section 54F of the Income Tax Act allows exemption from capital gains on sale of any long-term asset (including gold) if the proceeds are invested in a residential house property - subject to conditions. Consult a chartered accountant to see if you qualify.

Practical Tips

  • Sell the gold 3–5 working days before you need to pay the down payment - ensures funds clear comfortably
  • For very large amounts (above ₹20L), plan the sale a few days in advance
  • Keep the gold sale receipt - needed for ITR and potentially for Section 54F claim
  • Bring PAN card - virtually all down payment-level sales exceed ₹2,00,000
  • If selling multiple family members' gold, each person needs their own Aadhaar and PAN

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I sell gold and use the money for a down payment?

How much gold do I need for a ₹10 lakh down payment?

Approximately 72g of 22K gold at today's rate of ₹13,965/g.

Section 54F of the Income Tax Act may allow capital gains exemption if certain conditions are met. Consult a chartered accountant - this is a significant potential saving.

Can I pay my down payment in cash from gold sale?

Section 269ST prohibits cash payments above ₹2,00,000. Your builder/seller may not accept such large cash anyway. Bank transfer is the recommended route.

Do I need PAN to sell gold for a down payment?

Yes - virtually all down payment-level sales exceed ₹2,00,000, making PAN mandatory.

Should I sell all my gold at once or in parts?

For speed and simplicity, sell the required amount in one visit. Splitting into multiple visits for the same purpose does not provide any advantage.

html:
Using personal gold to fund business expenses or working capital is a centuries-old practice in India. Whether it is a cash flow emergency, a new machinery purchase, or seed capital for a startup, gold remains one of the fastest ways to raise funds outside of bank financing.

This guide covers the tax angle, compliance, and practical process.

At a Glance

Gold sale → business use?

Yes - sell gold, proceeds go to personal account, then transfer to business

Capital gains on gold sale?

Yes - 12.5% LTCG if held 24+ months

Can you deduct gold sale in business books?

No - gold sale is a personal capital transaction

GST on gold sale by individual?

No - individuals selling personal gold do not charge GST

Section 269ST cash limit

₹2,00,000 - large sales must be by bank transfer

Time to get funds

Same day - sell at branch, bank transfer within hours

The Process: Gold to Business Capital

  1. Payment by bank transfer to your personal account (mandatory if sale > ₹2,00,000)
  2. Transfer funds from your personal account to your business current account
  3. Book the transfer appropriately in your business accounts (loan from proprietor/director, or capital injection depending on business structure)
  4. Keep both the gold sale receipt and the transfer record for audit trail

Tax Implications

  • Capital gains tax on the gold sale: personal tax - 12.5% LTCG (gold held 24+ months) on the profit
  • The gold sale and the subsequent business use are two separate transactions for tax purposes
  • The capital gain is reported in your personal ITR under Schedule CG
  • The business injection is recorded as a loan or capital contribution in business books - no additional tax

Proprietors vs Pvt Ltd Directors

  • Proprietorship: gold sale proceeds can be directly brought in as capital - straightforward
  • Partnership firm: each partner can inject personal gold sale proceeds as capital
  • Pvt Ltd director: proceeds are injected as a loan to the company (director loan) - recorded in books
  • In all cases: the gold sale is a personal transaction; the company or firm receives the money as a transfer

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I sell personal gold to fund my business?

Is the capital gains tax on gold sale a business expense?

No - it is a personal tax on the gold sale. It is not a business deduction.

Do I charge GST when selling personal gold?

No - individuals selling personal jewellery do not levy GST.

Is a gold loan better than selling gold for business capital?

If you can repay within 3–6 months, a gold loan lets you reclaim the gold. If you need permanent capital, selling gives more money upfront without interest burden.

How fast can I get money from selling gold for my business?

Same day - sell at branch in 30 minutes, bank transfer within a few hours.

Can I deduct the cost of selling gold in my business accounts?

The gold sale is a personal transaction. You cannot deduct the gold's cost in your business books. The proceeds are an injection of personal capital.

What is the Section 269ST limit for gold sales?

You cannot receive more than ₹2,00,000 in cash for a single gold sale. Large amounts must be via bank transfer.

html:
Getting the best price for your gold is not about luck - it is about knowing the market rate, choosing the right buyer, and understanding what deductions are legitimate vs inflated.

Today's IBJA 22K rate is ₹13,965/g. A good seller should receive 97–99% of this. A seller who walks in unprepared may receive 92–95%. The difference on 50g of gold is more than ₹34,923.

At a Glance

Current 22K IBJA rate

₹13,965/g

Fair payout range

97–99% of IBJA rate

Red flag

More than 5% below IBJA without explanation

Most important step

Check the IBJA rate before you go

Second most important

Get at least 2 quotes before selling

Last Updated

May 2026

Step 1: Check the IBJA Rate Before You Leave Home

Go to ibja.co and note today's 22K (916) rate - currently ₹13,965/g. This is your benchmark. Any buyer who refuses to state their rate as a percentage of IBJA is a red flag.

Also calculate your approximate value: Weight × 0.916 × ₹15,250/g for 22K gold.

Step 2: Get at Least Two Quotes

Step 3: Insist on XRF Testing - Not Acid Tests

XRF (X-ray fluorescence) testing is non-destructive and gives a precise purity reading. Ask to see the XRF result on screen. Acid testing is less precise and can be manipulated. A buyer who refuses XRF or only acid tests is not transparent.

Step 4: Watch the Weighing

Stand at the counter and watch the weight shown on the digital scale. The scale should be zeroed (show 0.00g) before your gold is placed on it. Note the weight displayed - it should match what is written on your receipt.

Step 5: Understand Stone and Lac Deductions

  • Stones (rubies, diamonds, emeralds) are removed from the piece before weighing - this is correct
  • Lac (resin filling inside hollow bangles/chains): an amount is estimated and deducted - ask what weight is being deducted and why
  • If deductions seem excessive, ask for an explanation - a transparent buyer will show you how the deduction was calculated
  • Making charges are NOT deducted at resale - any buyer who deducts making charges is incorrectly reducing your payout

Step 6: Negotiate the Buyer Margin

Most buyers have a margin of 1–3% below IBJA. For large amounts (500g+), you can ask: 'What is your best rate per gram for this quantity?' Some buyers offer slightly better rates for large transactions.

Step 7: Verify the Receipt Before Accepting

  • Receipt should show: weight (grams), purity (% or karat), IBJA rate used, deductions itemised, and final amount
  • Compare the receipt figures to what the scale and XRF showed you
  • If anything does not match, ask before signing
  • Keep the receipt - you need it for ITR filing

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I get the best price when selling gold?

Check the IBJA rate first (ibja.co), get two quotes, insist on XRF testing, watch the weighing, verify deductions, and compare receipts before signing.

Who pays the most for gold in India?

Can I negotiate the gold rate at the branch?

For large amounts (500g+), some negotiation is possible. For standard retail amounts, the rate is typically fixed.

What deductions are legitimate when selling gold?

Stone weight, lac/resin filling weight. Making charges are NOT a legitimate deduction at resale.

Should I clean my gold before selling?

Not necessary - cleaning does not affect the rate. Bring it as-is.

What is the maximum I can receive for 22K gold?

The IBJA rate is ₹13,965/g. Reputable buyers pay 97–99% of this - i.e. ₹13,546–₹13,825/g.

Is it safe to sell gold at a branch alone?

title: Gold Melting Charges in India: What They Are & Who Actually Charges Them

source.intent: Process/consumer education: melting charges — common seller confusion, red flag awareness. Uncovered.

html:
'Melting charges' is a term some gold buyers use to justify deducting an additional amount from the gold sale price - above the standard buyer margin. For many sellers, especially those unfamiliar with the process, this sounds legitimate.

Here is the truth: reputable gold buyers do not charge separate melting fees to sellers. Here is why, and what to do if you encounter this practice.

At a Glance

Should a buyer charge you melting fees?

No - reputable buyers do not charge sellers for melting

Who absorbs refining/melting cost?

The buyer - covered within their 1–3% margin

Is a melting charge deduction legitimate?

Only if disclosed upfront and agreed - otherwise it is an inflated deduction

What to do if charged?

Ask for it in writing - then compare with another buyer

Last Updated

May 2026

What Is a Gold Melting Charge?

When jewellery is sold to a gold buyer, it eventually goes to a refinery where it is melted, assayed, and purified. The refinery charges the buyer for this process.

A 'melting charge' is when some buyers attempt to pass this refining cost on to you - the seller - by deducting it from your payout on top of their normal margin.

Typical melting charge claims: ₹50–₹200 per gram, or a flat ₹500–₹2,000 per transaction.

Why Reputable Buyers Do Not Charge Melting Fees

The buyer's 1–3% margin below the IBJA rate already covers:
• Refining and melting costs at their partner refinery
• Branch operating costs
• Testing equipment and consumables
• The buyer's profit margin

A buyer who charges both a margin below IBJA AND a separate melting fee is double-dipping - taking more than their declared margin. At today's rate of ₹13,965/g for 22K, a ₹100/g 'melting charge' on top of a 2% margin effectively makes their total deduction 2.7% - which should be disclosed upfront, not hidden as a separate fee.

When Melting Charges Are Legitimate

  • At refineries when you take gold directly for refining (bypassing a buyer) - refineries charge a refining fee of ₹30–₹100/g
  • When you send gold to be smelted and assayed and want the proceeds directly - refineries are different from gold buyers
  • For very unusual alloys (foreign gold, dental gold, industrial alloys) where assay is complex - a nominal extra charge may be disclosed and agreed upfront
  • Always ensure any such charge is disclosed before, not deducted after, the transaction is agreed

How to Respond If You Are Charged a Melting Fee

  • Ask: 'Why is there a separate melting charge on top of your rate?' - a transparent buyer can explain
  • Ask for it in writing on the receipt - if they refuse, that is a red flag
  • Compare: visit another buyer and see if they charge the same
  • Do the maths: include the melting charge in your effective per-gram cost and compare to the IBJA rate
  • You can walk away from a transaction before signing the receipt if the terms are not what you agreed

Frequently Asked Questions

Do gold buyers charge melting fees in India?

What is a fair gold melting charge?

For a standard seller: zero. Refining cost is covered by the buyer's margin. A separate melting fee on top of a margin deduction is not standard practice at certified gold buyers.

Can I refuse to pay a melting charge?

Yes - you can decline the transaction before signing if a melting charge is added without prior disclosure.

Are melting charges deducted from the weight or the rate?

Some buyers deduct melting loss from the weight (e.g. '3% melting loss from gross weight') - this is a different form of the same practice. Ask for a clear breakdown.

Is a stone removal charge the same as a melting charge?

No. Stone removal is a legitimate deduction of the stone's weight from the gold weight (the stone itself is returned or set aside). Melting charges are an additional fee on top of this.

What is the refinery charge if I sell directly to a refinery?

Refineries typically charge ₹30–₹100/g for assaying and refining. This is different from the melting charges some local buyers attempt to impose on retail sellers.

title: Why the Gold Rate Changes Twice a Day in India

source.title: Why Gold Rate Changes Twice a Day
source.intent: DIFFERENT INTENT from existing rate guides: explains the mechanics of IBJA dual publication — why two rates exist, the London fix connection, which applies to your transaction.

html:
If you check the gold rate at 10 AM and again at 6 PM, you will often see two different numbers - even though 'today's rate' sounds like it should be one figure. This is not an error. The IBJA (India Bullion and Jewellers Association) publishes the gold rate twice every working day, and understanding why helps you make smarter decisions about when to sell.

At a Glance

IBJA AM rate published

~11:30 AM on working days

IBJA PM rate published

~5:00 PM on working days

Why two rates?

Morning and evening London gold fixings are separate - IBJA follows both

Which rate do buyers use?

The most recently published rate at the time of your transaction

Do rates change often between AM and PM?

Yes - can differ by ₹50–₹300/10g depending on global market movement

Weekend rate?

Last published rate (PM on previous working day) applies

Last Updated

May 2026

The IBJA Rate Publication Schedule

The IBJA publishes two gold rates on every MCX (Multi Commodity Exchange) working day:

• AM rate: published around 11:30 AM IST
• PM rate: published around 5:00 PM IST

These correspond roughly to the two London Bullion Market Association (LBMA) gold price fixings that occur daily - the AM fixing at ~1:30 PM IST and the PM fixing at ~7:30 PM IST.

The IBJA takes the international gold price, converts it to INR using the live USD/INR exchange rate, adds import duty (15%), AGIF cess (3%), and other levies - then publishes the resulting domestic benchmark rate.

Why the AM and PM Rates Differ

Between 11:30 AM and 5:00 PM, the international gold market continues to trade. Global events - US economic data releases, Federal Reserve commentary, geopolitical news, oil price movements - can move the gold price by $10–$30/oz between fixings.

Converted to INR at current rates:
• $10/oz change ≈ ₹1.08/g ≈ ₹10.8 per 10g
• $30/oz change ≈ ₹3.25/g ≈ ₹32.5 per 10g

For a seller with 100g of 22K gold:
• A ₹30/g difference between AM and PM = ₹3,000 on the total payout

This is why knowing which rate applies to your transaction matters.

Which Rate Applies When You Sell?

Time of Your Visit

Rate That Applies

Before 11:30 AM

Previous day's PM rate (or last published rate)

11:30 AM to ~5:00 PM

That day's AM rate (most recently published)

After 5:00 PM (if buyer still open)

That day's PM rate

Weekend or holiday

Last working day's PM rate

Does It Matter Which Rate You Get?

For most sellers, the AM vs PM difference is small and unpredictable. You cannot know whether the PM rate will be higher or lower than the AM rate - the gold market moves in both directions.

The better strategy: if today's rate (either fixing) is at a level you are happy with, sell. Waiting for the PM rate hoping it will be higher is a 50/50 bet.

To check the current published IBJA rate before visiting: go to ibja.co and look at the most recent rate and its published time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does the gold rate update twice a day?

The IBJA follows two international gold price fixings (London AM and PM) and publishes domestic INR rates twice on each working day - at ~11:30 AM and ~5:00 PM IST.

Which gold rate applies when I sell - AM or PM?

The most recently published IBJA rate at the time you complete the transaction. Before 5 PM, the AM rate applies; after 5 PM, the PM rate.

Does the gold rate change significantly between morning and evening?

It can - differences of ₹50–₹300 per 10 grams are common depending on global market activity that day.

Should I sell in the morning or evening to get a better rate?

There is no reliable pattern. The PM rate can be higher or lower than the AM rate. Sell when the published rate is at a level you are comfortable with.

What rate applies on weekends?

The last published PM rate from the preceding working day.

Where can I check the current IBJA rate?

ibja.co - the official IBJA website, which shows the date and time of each published rate.

We use the most recently published IBJA rate at the time of your transaction.

html:
Selling gold for the first time is surprisingly stressful. You have a valuable asset, an unfamiliar process, and - if you go to the wrong buyer - the risk of getting significantly less than you should.

These are the 8 most common mistakes first-time gold sellers make. Avoiding them can make the difference of thousands of rupees on a typical sale.

At a Glance

Most expensive mistake

Not checking the IBJA rate before you go

Second costliest

Accepting the first quote without comparison

Biggest red flag

A buyer who won't show you the XRF reading

Most overlooked

Not watching the weighing display

Time at branch

20–35 minutes - no need to rush

Last Updated

May 2026

Mistake 1: Not Checking the IBJA Rate Before You Leave Home

The IBJA rate is the national benchmark - publicly available on ibja.co. If you walk in without knowing it, you have no way to evaluate whether the offer is fair.

Check today's 22K rate (currently ₹13,965/g) before your visit. Calculate your approximate value: weight × 0.916 × ₹15,250. Any offer more than 3% below this number deserves a question.

Mistake 2: Going to Only One Buyer

First-time sellers often assume the nearest buyer or the jeweller they bought from is the best choice. In most cases, a dedicated gold buyer pays 3–7% more than a jeweller for the same piece.

Get at least two quotes - it takes one extra visit but can add thousands of rupees to your payout on a 20–50g sale.

Mistake 3: Not Watching the Weighing Display

  • Stand at the counter and watch the digital scale display
  • Confirm the scale shows 0.00g before your gold is placed on it
  • Note the weight shown - it should match the weight on your receipt exactly
  • If the scale is turned away from you or you are asked to step back - that is a red flag

Mistake 4: Accepting a Purity Reading You Didn't See

Always ask to see the XRF result on the machine screen. A reputable buyer will show it to you without hesitation. If a buyer quotes a purity without showing you any testing result - or only does a colour test - be skeptical. XRF gives the number; colour tests are qualitative and less precise.

Mistake 5: Not Understanding What Is Deducted (and What Should Not Be)

  • Legitimate deductions: stone weight, lac/resin filling weight
  • NOT a legitimate deduction: making charges (these are a buying cost, not a selling deduction)
  • NOT a legitimate deduction: separate 'melting charges' on top of the buyer's margin
  • Ask for every deduction to be explained and listed on the receipt

Mistake 6: Selling Stone-Set Jewellery Without Understanding the Stone Deduction

If your jewellery has diamonds, rubies, emeralds or other stones, they will be removed (or estimated) before the gold is weighed. First-time sellers are sometimes surprised that a heavy-looking piece pays much less than expected because the stones account for 20–40% of the weight.

Bring plain gold pieces (chains, bangles) first if you want a simpler, faster first experience.

Mistake 7: Leaving Without a Receipt

Always take the receipt. It should show: weight, purity, IBJA rate used, deductions itemised, total amount paid, your Aadhaar number (last 4 digits), and date.

You need the receipt for ITR filing. Never leave without it.

Mistake 8: Waiting for the Perfect Rate

Gold rates move every day. Many first-time sellers delay their sale waiting for a 'better' rate. Gold is currently at ₹13,965/g for 22K - a historically strong level. If you have a need for the funds, waiting is speculation, not strategy. Sell at a rate you are comfortable with today.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the most important thing to do before selling gold for the first time?

Check the IBJA rate on ibja.co and calculate your approximate value. This gives you a benchmark to evaluate any offer.

Should I get multiple quotes when selling gold?

Yes - even two quotes (a dedicated gold buyer and a jeweller) often reveals a meaningful price difference.

What should I look for on a gold sale receipt?

Weight, purity %, IBJA rate used, each deduction itemised, total payout amount, Aadhaar details, and date of transaction.

What is a XRF test and should I see the result?

XRF is X-ray fluorescence - the precision method to confirm gold purity. Yes, always ask to see the result on the screen.

Can I sell gold with stones in it?

Yes - stones are removed or estimated and excluded from the gold weight. Expect the payout to be lower per gram than plain jewellery.

Is it safe to sell gold at a dedicated gold buyer?

How long does the first sale typically take?

30–45 minutes for a first-timer - slightly longer than subsequent visits as you will want to verify each step.

html:
Your necklace has been repaired, a ring has been resized, or a clasp has been replaced. Now you want to sell the piece. A common question: does the repair affect the gold's purity - and therefore what you receive?

The answer depends entirely on how the repair was done and what materials were used. Here is a clear breakdown.

At a Glance

Can repair affect purity?

Yes - if non-gold solder or base metal repairs were used

Traditional solder (KDM/cadmium)

Can reduce purity in the repair area

Modern gold solder

Same karat as base metal - purity unchanged

Resizing (stretching/compressing)

Does not affect purity - same gold throughout

Polishing / rhodium plating

Does not affect purity

XRF will detect the difference?

Yes - XRF tests the actual gold area, not just the surface

Last Updated

May 2026

How Different Types of Repair Affect Purity

Repair Type

Purity Impact

What XRF Shows

Resizing (stretching ring)

None - same metal

Same karat as original

Resizing (cutting and soldering)

Possible - depends on solder used

XRF tests the solder join

Gold solder (same karat)

None - solder matches base metal karat

Same karat throughout

Silver solder

Reduces purity at join

XRF shows lower gold% near join

KDM/cadmium solder (old method, pre-2000)

Reduces purity and adds cadmium

XRF may show cadmium and lower gold%

Lac filling (for weight)

Not purity but weight fraud

XRF cannot detect lac - weighing does

Rhodium plating (white gold)

None to purity

XRF penetrates plating to gold below

Polishing

None

Unaffected

The KDM Era: Why Old Repaired Jewellery Tests Lower

Before the BIS banned cadmium-based solder in India (around 2000–2001), most jewellers used KDM solder - a cadmium-tin alloy - to join gold pieces. Cadmium is significantly cheaper than gold and lowers the overall gold content of the piece wherever it was used.

This is why many pieces of jewellery repaired before 2000 test at 20K–21K rather than the expected 22K. The cadmium solder mixed with the gold at the repair points pulls down the average purity reading.

XRF testing is honest about this - it reports the actual composition. A piece that XRF-reads at 87% gold (≈21K) is paid at the 21K rate, regardless of what the original hallmark said.

What Happens During XRF Testing of Repaired Jewellery

  • XRF tests a specific spot on the piece - the result reflects the composition at that point
  • If the tester tests at the solder join, a lower gold% may show
  • If the tester tests on the main body of the piece away from any join, the result reflects the base metal purity
  • Reputable buyers test multiple spots and use the average, or test the main body
  • Ask where the XRF probe was placed - this matters for repaired pieces

What to Do If Your Gold Was Repaired

  • Tell the branch staff that the piece has been repaired - they can test multiple spots
  • Ask what karat the repair material was - a jeweller who used same-karat gold solder can confirm this
  • If the repair was done professionally with same-karat gold solder, purity should be unchanged
  • If you suspect old KDM solder was used, expect the XRF to show slightly lower purity

Frequently Asked Questions

Does repairing gold reduce its value?

Only if the repair used lower-purity or non-gold solder. Modern gold-to-gold repair with same-karat solder should not reduce purity.

What is KDM solder and why does it affect purity?

KDM solder contained cadmium - a cheaper metal - which was used to join gold pieces before 2001. It reduces the overall gold content in the repaired area.

Can XRF detect soldering?

Yes - XRF identifies the composition wherever the probe is placed, including solder joints. A cadmium or silver solder join will show clearly in the result.

If my jewellery was resized, does the purity change?

Resizing by stretching or compressing changes the shape but not the purity. Resizing by cutting and re-joining (with solder) may affect purity depending on the solder used.

Does rhodium plating affect gold purity?

No - rhodium plating is a surface treatment that does not change the gold alloy beneath. XRF penetrates the plating and reads the gold content correctly.

What should I tell the branch when selling repaired jewellery?

Mention that the piece has been repaired. The staff will test at multiple points to ensure an accurate purity assessment.

Why does my old gold test at 20K when I thought it was 22K?

Old KDM solder (pre-2001) commonly contains cadmium that dilutes the gold content. This is one of the most common reasons old pieces test below their expected purity.

MMTC-PAMP coins come in tamper-proof cards with a unique serial number and Swiss certification. When the seal is unbroken, a buyer can verify authenticity without XRF testing.

• Faster processing at the branch
• No doubt raised about purity
• Same per-gram rate as any other certified 24K coin: ₹15,250/g

Once the tamper-proof card is opened or damaged, XRF testing is required - same as any other coin.

Does Brand Affect the Per-Gram Rate?

No - per gram, all confirmed 24K coins receive the same IBJA rate: ₹15,250/g. The brand affects:
• How quickly the transaction processes (sealed MMTC-PAMP is fastest)

Which gold coin is best for resale in India?

Gold coins have no making charges and no stone deductions. At resale, you receive the full per-gram gold value. Jewellery may be more sentimental but making charges are not recovered.

Can I sell any gold coin regardless of country of origin?

Yes - XRF testing determines purity regardless of origin. You are paid based on tested gold content.

How much does the gold rate change per week in India?

In a typical week: ₹100–₹400 per gram for 22K. In high-volatility weeks (US Fed, geopolitical events): ₹500–₹1,500 per gram.

Is gold rate predictable week to week?

Should I wait a week before selling gold?

US Federal Reserve decisions, US jobs data (NFP), inflation data (CPI), geopolitical crises (wars, sanctions), and Indian budget import duty changes.

What is the best time within a week to sell gold?

There is no statistically reliable pattern within a week. Sell when the rate is at a level you are comfortable with.

keywords.keyword: why gold tests lower than expected
old gold purity lower xrf india

html:
You bring a piece of gold that the family has always called '22K' to the branch. The XRF test comes back at 87% (≈21K). You are confused and perhaps suspicious.

This situation is extremely common with old jewellery - and in most cases, it is not the result of cheating. There are 7 legitimate, well-understood reasons why old gold tests below its expected purity.

At a Glance

Most common cause

KDM/cadmium solder used in old repairs (pre-2001)

Second most common

Jeweller originally sold below-marked purity (pre-BIS mandatory)

Does lower XRF mean cheating at the branch?

Almost never - XRF accurately reads what is there

What rate do you get?

The rate for the tested purity - not the expected purity

Can you dispute it?

Yes - ask for multiple tests at different spots

Last Updated

May 2026

7 Reasons Old Gold Tests Below Expected Purity

  1. KDM/Cadmium Solder: Before 2001, most repairs used KDM solder - a cadmium-tin alloy cheaper than gold. Cadmium dilutes the gold% wherever it was used. A 22K piece repaired twice with KDM solder can test at 20–21K.
  2. Original under-purity at manufacture: Before BIS mandatory hallmarking (June 2021), jewellers were not legally required to verify purity. Some sold pieces at 20–21K purity while calling them '22K'. Without mandatory XRF/hallmarking at purchase, there was no check.
  3. Mixing gold of different purities: Old jewellery sets were sometimes assembled by combining pieces of different karats. A necklace with 22K gold and an 18K pendant combined might average 21K.
  4. Repair with lower-karat gold: A repair done with 18K gold on a 22K piece lowers the average purity wherever the repair material is present.
  5. Surface oxidation or deposits: Heavy surface oxidation can sometimes affect XRF readings slightly - though modern XRF machines are designed to compensate for this.
  6. Silver solder at join points: Some repairs used silver solder (not gold-based). Silver has lower density and significantly lower value than gold - any silver solder pulls down the gold% reading.
  7. Internal lac or resin not detected by XRF: Lac filling inside hollow bangles/chains adds weight but no gold value. XRF identifies the gold content of the metal itself - but the presence of lac makes the total weight higher than the gold weight alone.

What to Do If Your Gold Tests Lower Than Expected

  • Ask the branch staff to test at multiple spots - the main body, a joining area, a pendant connection
  • The spot with the least repair/solder work typically gives the highest reading
  • If the reading is significantly below 22K (below 88%), ask for an explanation - which areas tested lower and why
  • You can get a second opinion - bring the piece to another branch or certified testing centre
  • Ultimately, you are paid for the actual gold content confirmed by XRF - this is the accurate number

Is It the Branch Cheating You?

In the overwhelming majority of cases: no. XRF machines at certified branches are calibrated and cannot easily be manipulated. The reading is what the piece actually contains.

The rare exception: a branch testing at a solder join point specifically (lowest gold area) to undervalue the piece. This is why asking to see the XRF probe location and requesting multiple spot tests matters.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did my 22K gold test at only 20K or 21K?

Most commonly: old KDM cadmium solder used in repairs before 2001. Also possible: original manufacture below stated purity, or mixing of gold purities in the piece.

Is the branch cheating me with a lower XRF reading?

In almost all cases, no. XRF accurately reads the gold content. The lower result reflects the actual composition, often due to old solder.

What rate do I receive if my gold tests at 21K instead of 22K?

You receive the 21K rate - which is the rate for 87.5% pure gold. This is less than the 22K rate but reflects what is actually in the piece.

Can I get a second opinion on the XRF reading?

Yes - you can visit another branch or a certified assay centre. The result should be consistent within ±0.5% if the equipment is properly calibrated.

What is KDM solder and why does it reduce purity?

KDM solder contained cadmium, a cheaper metal used in gold repairs before 2001. It was banned by BIS but its use in old pieces is widespread.

How do I know if my piece was repaired with KDM solder?

There is no visual indicator. XRF testing at the join points will typically show cadmium content if KDM solder was used.

Is old gold worth less per gram than new gold?

Only if it tests at lower purity. If an old piece tests at 91.6% (22K), it receives the same rate as new 22K gold.

title: Why India Uses 22K Gold (Not 18K Like Europe): The Historical Reason
metaTitle: Why India Uses 22K Gold Not 18K | Historical & Cultural Reason Explained

source.intent: DIFFERENT INTENT from 22K purity guide: historical/cultural WHY — explains the economic and cultural logic behind India's 22K preference vs global norms.

html:
Walk into any jewellery shop in India and you will find 22K gold - 91.6% pure, deep yellow, heavy for its size. Walk into a European jewellery shop and you will find 18K or even 14K gold. Why the difference?

The answer is part history, part culture, and part practicality - and understanding it gives you a clearer picture of why 22K gold resells so well in India while 18K takes a significant per-gram value cut.

At a Glance

Indian standard

22K (916 hallmark) - 91.6% pure gold

European standard

18K (750) or 14K (585)

Gulf standard

21K (875)

USA standard

14K (585) or 10K (417)

Why 22K in India?

Cultural preference for high-purity gold + investment store-of-value

Resale implication

22K gets the highest per-gram rate of any wearable gold karat

Last Updated

May 2026

The Historical Reason: Gold as Savings, Not Just Jewellery

In Indian culture, gold jewellery has never been purely ornamental. For centuries - and even today - gold serves as:
• A savings instrument (liquid wealth outside the banking system)
• A dowry asset transferred between families at marriage
• An emergency fund realisable in any market condition
• A trust asset preserved across generations

When gold is used as savings, purity matters enormously. A family jeweller who mixed the gold with too many alloys was reducing the family's stored wealth. The cultural preference for high purity gold is therefore deeply rational - it is about maximising the store-of-value function.

Europe, by contrast, developed a different relationship with jewellery - more aesthetic, more fashion-forward, less savings-oriented. 18K and 14K are harder, more durable, and better for delicate stone settings. European jewellery culture optimised for design; Indian gold culture optimised for value density.

The Practical Reason: Resale and Liquidity

22K gold has a near-frictionless resale market in India. Every gold buyer, every jeweller and every household recognises the 916 hallmark. The IBJA rate is published daily for 22K specifically.

At resale:
• 22K piece, 10g: ₹1,39,690
• 18K piece, 10g: ₹1,14,375
• 14K piece, 10g: ₹89,212

The per-gram value of 22K vs 18K is a meaningful difference (₹2,527/g at today's rates). For a family holding 500g of gold, the difference between 22K and 18K is ₹11,57,366 in total value. High purity = higher stored value = preferred in India.

Why European Gold Uses Lower Karats

  • 18K and 14K are harder than 22K - better for setting diamonds and stones precisely
  • Lower karat = less gold cost = lower jewellery prices = more accessible fashion market
  • European jewellery historically emphasised design and craftsmanship premium over gold content
  • Investment gold (bars, coins) in Europe is 24K - they separate jewellery from investment; India typically does not
  • Lower karat gold is more durable for everyday wear (22K scratches more easily)

What This Means When You Sell

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does India use 22K gold instead of 18K?

Cultural preference for high-purity gold as a store of value, emergency fund, and dowry asset. 22K maximises gold content per gram - more value density for the family holding it.

Is 22K gold better than 18K?

It depends on purpose. For investment/resale: 22K is better (higher gold content per gram). For stone-set jewellery or durability: 18K is better (harder, more design-friendly).

Can I sell 18K gold in India?

Yes - at the 18K rate ({inr(R18)}/g). Less per gram than 22K, but fully acceptable at certified gold buyers.

Why is European gold jewellery lower purity?

European jewellery culture optimised for design, durability and fashion - not investment storage. 18K and 14K are harder and better for setting stones.

Does the Gulf use the same purity as India?

No - Gulf countries (Dubai, Bahrain, Oman) typically use 21K (875 hallmark). Higher than Europe but slightly below India's 22K standard.

Is 24K jewellery common in India?

No - 24K is too soft for everyday jewellery. It is used for investment coins, biscuits and bars. 22K strikes the balance between high purity and workability.

Why is 22K gold resale so easy in India?

Because the 22K (916) hallmark is universally recognised, the IBJA publishes daily 22K rates, and the entire gold market infrastructure is built around this purity standard.

If you have received an auction notice for your pledged gold, you are in a time-sensitive situation. A gold loan auction notice means the lender is about to sell your gold to recover the outstanding loan amount.

This guide explains exactly what the notice means, what your options are, and how much time you typically have to act.

At a Glance

What is a gold loan auction?

Lender sells your pledged gold to recover the outstanding amount if you default

Notice period required

RBI mandates a minimum of 30 days' notice before auction in most cases

Can you stop the auction?

Yes - by repaying the outstanding amount or refinancing before the auction date

What happens if gold is auctioned?

What if auction proceeds are less than dues?

What Triggers a Gold Loan Auction Notice?

  • Non-payment of EMIs or interest for 90+ days (NPA classification)
  • Loan tenure expiry without renewal or repayment
  • LTV (Loan-to-Value) ratio breach - if gold price falls and the outstanding loan exceeds 75–85% of gold value
  • Repeated missed payments after multiple reminder notices
  • NBFC and bank timelines vary - check your loan agreement for the specific default clause

What Happens When the Gold Is Auctioned

The lender conducts a public auction - typically in person at the branch or via a registered auctioneer. RBI regulations require:
• Minimum 30 days' notice to the borrower
• Auction to be conducted at fair market value
• Any surplus over the outstanding dues + charges must be returned to the borrower

Example: Outstanding loan ₹1,50,000. Auction proceeds ₹2,79,380 (20g 22K). Charges ₹15,000.
Surplus = ₹2,79,380 − ₹1,50,000 − ₹15,000 = ₹1,14,380 returned to you.

If auction proceeds are less than the total outstanding: you may still owe the shortfall, depending on the lender and your loan agreement.

Immediate Steps to Take

  1. Read the notice carefully - note the auction date and time
  2. Contact the lender immediately to discuss your options
  3. Ask for a full statement of outstanding: principal, accrued interest, penalties
  4. Calculate whether you can repay from any source (savings, family, selling other assets)
  5. If refinancing: approach another gold loan lender with your auction notice - some lenders specifically offer top-up/takeover for this scenario
  6. If you cannot repay: attend the auction - you can bid to re-purchase your own gold

Frequently Asked Questions

What does a gold loan auction notice mean?

It means the lender is about to sell your pledged gold to recover the outstanding loan amount due to default.

How much time do I have after receiving an auction notice?

RBI regulations require minimum 30 days' notice before auction for most lenders. Check your specific notice for the auction date.

Can I stop the gold loan auction?

Yes - by repaying the full outstanding amount (principal + interest + charges) before the auction date.

What happens to any excess money from the auction?

If auction proceeds exceed the outstanding dues and charges, the surplus must be returned to you under RBI guidelines.

Can I buy my own gold back at the auction?

Yes - you can attend the auction and bid for your own gold. The lender cannot legally prevent you from participating.

Can I take a new gold loan to repay an old one?

Yes - some lenders specifically offer gold loan takeover products. You would use a new loan from a second lender to repay the first.

What if auction proceeds are less than my dues?

You may still owe the shortfall to the lender, depending on your loan agreement terms. Get legal advice if this situation arises.

html:
India is often called 'the land of gold' - and with good reason. Indian households hold an estimated 25,000 to 30,000 tonnes of gold, the largest private gold stock of any country in the world. But what does this mean at the individual household level?

This guide breaks down the data and gives context to help you understand where your own gold holding fits in the broader picture.

At a Glance

India's estimated private gold stock

25,000–30,000 tonnes (WGC estimates)

India's share of world gold above ground

~12–14%

Average gold per household (urban India)

~200–500g (varies widely)

Average gold per household (rural India)

~100–250g (primarily jewellery)

India's annual gold demand

700–900 tonnes/year (WGC data)

Who holds the most gold in India?

South India - Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala

Last Updated

May 2026

India's Gold Stock: The Numbers

According to the World Gold Council (WGC), Indian households hold approximately 25,000–30,000 tonnes of gold - more than any other country. Germany's official gold reserves are approximately 3,352 tonnes; the US Federal Reserve holds approximately 8,133 tonnes. Indian private households collectively hold more gold than any central bank in the world.

In value terms at current rates:
25,000 tonnes = 25,000,000 kg = 25,000,000,000 grams
25 billion grams × ₹15,250/g = approximately ₹3,81,25,000 crore

This is an astronomical number - larger than India's annual GDP.

Regional Distribution of Gold Ownership in India

Urban households + wedding culture

Bhori-measured gold, temple traditions

Northeast India

Significant tribal gold traditions

What the Average Indian Household Holds

National averages mask enormous variation:

• Urban middle-class family (South India): 300–600g across all forms (jewellery, coins, biscuits)
• Rural agricultural household: 100–250g (primarily jewellery - generational)
• High-net-worth family: 1,000g+ (mix of jewellery, bars, and investment gold)
• Young urban professional: 20–100g (typically coins or digital gold)

At today's 22K rate of ₹13,965/g:
• 200g of 22K gold = ₹27,93,800
• 500g of 22K gold = ₹69,84,500
• 1 kg of 22K gold = ₹1,39,69,000

For most middle-class South Indian families, their gold holding represents a significant portion of their net worth.

Why India Holds So Much Gold

  • Cultural heritage: gold as dowry, inheritance and rite-of-passage gift is millennia-old
  • Distrust of financial systems: gold is seen as a store of value outside banks and government
  • Inflation hedge: historically, gold in INR has outpaced India's inflation rate
  • Liquidity: gold can be sold or pledged quickly without paperwork or credit check
  • Social signalling: visible gold ownership reflects family status in wedding and social contexts

Frequently Asked Questions

How much gold does the average Indian family own?

Estimates vary widely. A typical middle-class urban South Indian family may hold 200–500g across all forms. Rural households typically hold 100–250g.

How much gold does India as a country hold?

Indian households collectively hold an estimated 25,000–30,000 tonnes of gold - the largest private gold stock in the world.

Which state in India holds the most gold?

South Indian states - Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Kerala - collectively hold the highest proportion of India's private gold stock.

Why do Indians hold so much gold?

Cultural tradition (dowry, inheritance, religious), trust in gold as inflation hedge, liquidity advantages, and social signalling.

Is Indian household gold a good measure of the country's wealth?

Gold forms a significant part of household wealth, especially in rural and semi-urban India where formal financial products are less accessible.

Where does all this Indian gold come from?

Primarily imports - India imports 700–900 tonnes of gold annually. Some is recycled domestic gold.

Is there a limit on how much gold an Indian household can hold?

No absolute legal limit, but CBDT guidelines exempt specific amounts from documentation requirements during income tax searches: 500g (married women), 250g (unmarried women), 100g (men).

html:
On the evening of 8 November 2016, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1,000 currency notes. Within hours, gold buying queues formed at jewellery shops across India, and the gold rate saw one of its sharpest short-term spikes in recent history.

What actually happened to the gold rate, and why does demonetisation remain one of the most instructive events in India's gold market history?

At a Glance

Demonetisation date

8 November 2016

Notes demonetised

₹500 and ₹1,000 currency notes

Pre-demonetisation 22K rate

Approximately ₹2,800–₹3,000/g

Rate on 8–10 November 2016

Spiked to ₹3,600–₹4,200/g (intraday premiums even higher)

Peak premium over IBJA

Some shops charging 20–30% over IBJA rate in cash

Rate correction

Within 2–3 weeks, rate returned to ₹2,850–₹3,050/g

Last Updated

May 2026

Why Gold Spiked Immediately After Demonetisation

  • Sudden demand surge: People holding ₹500/₹1,000 notes rushed to convert cash to gold before the deadline
  • Gold is non-traceable (in the short term): Buyers hoped gold would not attract IT scrutiny the way large bank deposits would
  • Fear and uncertainty: Classic safe-haven buying during economic disruption
  • Supply constraint: Jewellers quickly ran out of stock as demand overwhelmed normal supply
  • Premium pricing: With high demand and limited stock, jewellers charged 15–30% above IBJA - far above the normal 1–3% margin

What Happened to Sellers During Demonetisation

For people trying to sell gold during this period, the situation was complicated:

• Officially, the IBJA rate barely changed - the benchmark stayed near ₹2,800–₹3,000/g
• But gold buyers became more selective - preferring not to buy if they could not resell immediately at a premium
• Some buyers offered slightly below the IBJA rate, citing uncertainty about banking
• Bank transfers were disrupted - payment for large gold sales was complicated by banking restrictions

Sellers who needed immediate cash during demonetisation found the process slower and more complicated than usual.

What Demonetisation Teaches About Gold's Safe-Haven Role

  • Gold demand spikes during economic disruption and currency crises
  • Physical gold is seen as outside the banking system - 'unaffected' by currency policy
  • Short-term gold premiums over IBJA can emerge in panic situations
  • The spike was temporary - rates normalised within weeks as panic subsided
  • Long-term, demonetisation had limited lasting impact on the gold price trend
  • IT crackdown: Purchases above ₹2L during demonetisation were flagged - many large cash-for-gold transactions attracted income tax notices later

Key Regulatory Response

The Income Tax department later identified gold purchases made with demonetised notes as potential undisclosed income. This led to tax notices for many buyers who had purchased large amounts in cash during November–December 2016.

The episode reinforced the importance of documented, KYC-compliant gold transactions.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened to the gold rate during demonetisation?

The official IBJA rate saw a modest uptick, but actual transaction premiums were 15–30% above IBJA at some shops as panicked buyers converted cash to gold.

Why did people rush to buy gold during demonetisation?

People sought to convert demonetised currency notes to gold before they became valueless - gold is a tangible, portable store of value.

Did the gold rate stay high after demonetisation?

No - the spike was short-lived. Within 2–3 weeks, the gold rate returned to pre-demonetisation levels as the panic subsided.

Were gold purchases during demonetisation tracked by income tax?

Yes - purchases above ₹2L required PAN, and many large cash purchases of gold attracted income tax scrutiny.

What is the current gold rate compared to demonetisation?

At demonetisation, 22K was approximately ₹2,800–₹3,000/g. Today it is ₹13,965/g - approximately 4.8x higher.

What does demonetisation tell us about gold?

That gold is treated as a safe-haven asset during economic disruption. When currency reliability is questioned, gold demand rises sharply.

Should I sell gold now or wait for another panic like demonetisation?

Demonetisation-style events are impossible to predict. Today's gold rate is at historically strong levels - selling for a need you have today is more reliable than speculating on a future crisis.

html:
You check the gold rate on a financial app and see 'MCX Gold: ₹X per 10g'. Then you check ibja.co and see a different number. Which one applies when you sell your gold?

The two rates are related but serve different purposes. Understanding the difference prevents confusion - and occasional frustration - when you arrive at a branch.

At a Glance

MCX gold rate

Futures market price - what traders pay for gold to be delivered in the future

IBJA gold rate

Spot benchmark - what applies to physical gold transactions today

Which applies to selling?

IBJA rate - not MCX directly

Are they related?

Yes - IBJA derives from international spot price influenced by MCX futures

Typical difference

MCX may be ₹50–₹200/10g higher than IBJA (futures premium)

Key question to ask buyer

"What is your rate as a % of IBJA today?" - not MCX

Last Updated

May 2026

What Is the MCX Gold Rate?

The MCX (Multi Commodity Exchange) is India's largest commodity exchange. Gold is traded on MCX as futures contracts - agreements to buy/sell a fixed quantity of gold (typically 1 kg) at a specified price on a future date.

The MCX gold rate is therefore the futures price - what market participants agree today for gold to be delivered in the next settlement month (typically the nearest active contract: current month, next month, or the month after).

MCX is where institutional buyers, jewellers who hedge inventory, and commodity traders participate. The MCX rate is the most visible gold price on Indian financial apps.

What Is the IBJA Rate?

Why MCX and IBJA Differ

Factor

MCX Rate

IBJA Rate

Type

Futures price (contract for future delivery)

Spot/physical price (today)

Includes carrying cost?

Yes - interest + storage for future months

No

Includes import duty?

Partially (via arbitrage)

Yes, fully baked in

Published when?

Continuously during market hours

Twice daily (~11:30 AM, ~5 PM)

Used for physical sales?

No - reference only

Yes - primary benchmark

Typical level vs each other

MCX usually 0.5–2% higher than IBJA

Lower than MCX

The Practical Rule for Sellers

When selling physical gold:
• Always use the IBJA rate (ibja.co) as your benchmark
• Today's IBJA 22K rate: ₹13,965/g
• Ask the buyer: "What % of IBJA are you paying for 22K today?"
• A fair answer: 97–99% of IBJA

Do not compare the buyer's rate to the MCX price - the MCX futures price is higher than the IBJA spot rate, and a buyer paying 'less than MCX' may actually be paying a fair rate relative to IBJA.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which gold rate should I use when selling - MCX or IBJA?

Use the IBJA rate. The IBJA is the physical gold spot benchmark - what buyers use. MCX is a futures market price, not directly applicable to physical sales.

Why is the MCX gold rate higher than the IBJA rate?

MCX prices include carrying costs (interest + storage) for future delivery. IBJA is a spot price for immediate physical gold. The premium varies by contract month.

Can I demand the MCX rate from a gold buyer?

No - MCX is a futures price, not a spot buying rate. Gold buyers use IBJA as their benchmark.

How are MCX and IBJA related?

The international spot price drives both. IBJA converts spot to INR with import duty; MCX futures reflect the spot plus carrying cost plus domestic supply-demand factors.

Does the MCX rate affect IBJA?

Indirectly yes - large moves in MCX futures are often a leading indicator of where the IBJA spot rate will move in the next publication.

What is a fair buyer rate relative to IBJA?

97–99% of IBJA for reputable buyers. Below 95% warrants questions.

Where do I find the IBJA rate?

ibja.co - the official IBJA website, published twice on working days.

html:
2020 was an extraordinary year for gold. As the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted global economies, locked down countries and sent stock markets crashing, gold delivered its strongest single-year performance in over a decade.

For Indian gold holders, 2020 was the year many long-held pieces more than doubled in INR value. Here is what actually happened, and what it teaches us.

At a Glance

22K rate in January 2020

Approximately ₹4,100/g

22K rate at August 2020 peak

Approximately ₹5,700–₹5,900/g (all-time high at the time)

22K rate today

₹13,965/g - even higher than 2020 peak

Why gold spiked in 2020

Global recession fears, Fed rate cuts, USD weakness, safe-haven demand

Lockdown impact on selling

Branches closed during lockdown - online gold sales rose

Last Updated

May 2026

The COVID Gold Rate Timeline in India

Period

22K Rate (approx)

Key Event

Pre-pandemic levels

March 2020

COVID declared pandemic; initial market panic

India lockdown; gold branches closed; online sales rise

July 2020

US Fed rate cut to near zero; global recession fear

August 2020 (peak)

₹5,700–₹5,900/g

All-time high at the time; global gold at $2,000+/oz

December 2020

Vaccine news; some safe-haven selling

2021 correction

₹4,500–₹4,800/g

Recovery optimism; gold gives back some gains

Why COVID Pushed Gold to All-Time Highs

  • Central bank rate cuts: The US Federal Reserve cut rates to near zero - lower rates reduce the opportunity cost of holding gold (which pays no interest)
  • Dollar weakening: COVID economic stimulus weakened the USD - gold (priced in USD) rose
  • Safe-haven demand: Global investors fled equities and bought gold as uncertainty peaked
  • India specifically: Rupee depreciation amplified the USD gold rise in INR terms
  • Supply disruption: Gold refineries and logistics were disrupted - temporary supply tightness

What Indian Gold Sellers Experienced in 2020

For sellers, 2020 presented an extraordinary opportunity. A family holding 500g of 22K gold:
• January 2020 value: ~₹69,84,500 (at ₹4,100/g)
• August 2020 value: ~₹26,56,400 (at ₹5,800/g)
• Gain in 8 months: ~₹7,78,600

However, many sellers could not access gold buyers during the April–May lockdown as branches were closed. Some sellers who waited until late 2021 received lower rates than the August 2020 peak.

What COVID Teaches About Gold's Role

  • Gold is a crisis asset - it typically rises when equities fall
  • Gold rewards patience - those who held through the 2008 or 2013 corrections eventually saw new highs
  • Liquidity risk is real - during severe lockdowns, even liquid assets like physical gold become illiquid if buyers are inaccessible
  • The COVID peak of ₹5,900/g in 2020 has now been significantly surpassed - gold in INR has continued its long-term upward trend
  • For sellers: selling at a 'good' rate is always relative to where you came from - at ₹13,965/g today, the 2020 peak buyer looks like a bargain

Frequently Asked Questions

What was the gold rate during COVID in India?

22K gold peaked at approximately ₹5,700–₹5,900/g in August 2020 - the highest it had ever been at that point. Today's rate of ₹13,965 is significantly higher.

Why did gold prices rise during COVID?

US Federal Reserve rate cuts, dollar weakening, safe-haven demand, and rupee depreciation all contributed to pushing gold to record highs in 2020.

Could I sell gold during the COVID lockdown?

Not during the strictest lockdown periods (April–May 2020) when non-essential businesses were closed. Branches reopened in a phased manner from May 2020 onwards.

Has the gold rate returned to pre-COVID levels?

No - gold has continued to rise well above COVID-era levels. The 2020 peak of ~₹5,900/g is now far below the current rate.

Is gold a good investment during economic crises?

Historically yes - gold tends to perform strongly during recessions, pandemics, and currency crises. COVID 2020 is a clear example.

What should I learn from 2020 gold performance?

Gold rewards long-term holders and provides crisis protection. But timing the perfect sell point is difficult - the 2020 peak sellers who got out at ₹5,900/g have missed further gains.

What is the gold rate today vs the 2020 peak?

2020 peak: ~₹5,900/g (22K). Today: ₹13,965/g - significantly higher.

title: Gold Smuggling Penalties in India: What Counts as Smuggling & Consequences
metaTitle: Gold Smuggling Penalties India | What Counts & What Are the Consequences

source.title: Gold Smuggling Penalties in India
source.intent: NEW TOPIC: Gold smuggling definition, penalties, difference from legitimate import — consumer education for NRIs and travellers. Not covered anywhere.

html:
India's customs authorities seize thousands of kilograms of smuggled gold annually. The consequences for gold smuggling are severe - and what many travellers do not realise is that simply failing to declare gold above the duty-free limit at the airport can be treated as smuggling.

This guide explains clearly what constitutes gold smuggling, what the penalties are, and how it differs from legitimate gold import.

At a Glance

Legal gold import

Declared at customs, duty paid on excess above free limits

Gold smuggling definition

Importing gold without declaration or with false declaration, or concealing gold

Minimum penalty

Equal to the value of the smuggled gold

Maximum penalty

3x the value + imprisonment in serious cases

Governing law

Customs Act 1962 + COFEPOSA in serious cases

Duty-free limits

Male NRI: 20g/₹50K | Female NRI: 40g/₹1L

Last Updated

May 2026

What Legally Constitutes Gold Smuggling in India

  • Bringing gold above the duty-free limit without declaring it at customs
  • Concealing gold in baggage, clothing, body, or freight
  • Making a false declaration about the quantity or value of gold being imported
  • Purchasing gold from smuggled stock (aiding and abetting smuggling)
  • Exporting gold without required documentation (less common for individuals)

Penalties Under the Customs Act 1962

Violation

Penalty Range

Additional Consequences

Undeclared gold above duty-free limit

100–300% of evaded duty

Gold may be confiscated; compounding option available

Concealed gold (deliberate)

1–3x value of confiscated gold

Criminal prosecution possible; COFEPOSA detention

Commercial-scale smuggling

3x value + imprisonment

COFEPOSA preventive detention (up to 1 year without trial)

False declaration

100–200% of underpaid duty

May bar future travel; passport flagged

Legitimate Import vs Smuggling - The Line

The key distinction is declaration:

• Legitimate import: You bring 60g of gold jewellery (above the 40g female limit). You go to the Red Channel, declare all 60g, and pay customs duty on the 20g excess. This is fully legal.

• Smuggling: You bring 60g but go through the Green Channel hoping not to be detected. If caught, the entire 60g may be confiscated and you face 100–300% penalty on the evaded duty.

The fine is not just on the excess - it can be on the entire value if concealment is found.

What to Do If You Accidentally Exceeded the Limit

  • Before boarding in the departure country: check your gold weight against current limits
  • At Indian airport if you realise you are over the limit: proceed to the Red Channel voluntarily and declare - voluntary disclosure is treated more leniently
  • If asked by customs officers after Green Channel passage: full cooperation and honest disclosure is the best approach
  • If gold is seized: get the seizure receipt and memorandum number; consult a customs lawyer for compounding (paying a settlement amount to recover the gold without prosecution)

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the penalty for gold smuggling in India?

100–300% of the evaded customs duty for undeclared gold; up to 3x the gold's value for deliberate concealment. Gold may also be permanently confiscated.

Is bringing gold above the limit from Dubai automatically smuggling?

Only if you don't declare it. Declare the excess at the Red Channel and pay duty - this is legal import, not smuggling.

Can confiscated gold be recovered?

Yes, through a legal process called compounding - you pay a settlement amount (fine + duty) and the gold is returned without criminal prosecution. Consult a customs lawyer.

What is COFEPOSA?

The Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act - allows preventive detention without trial for up to 1 year for serious smuggling offences.

How does customs detect hidden gold?

X-ray scanning, body scanners, physical search, intelligence inputs, and profiling at major international airports.

If I inherited gold from abroad and bring it to India, is that smuggling?

Not if you declare it at customs and pay the applicable duty on amounts above the duty-free limit.

What happens if I accidentally go through the Green Channel with excess gold?

Customs officers may search and find the excess. Voluntary disclosure before detection is treated far more leniently than discovery after search. Always use the Red Channel if in doubt.

html:
The US Federal Reserve meets eight times a year and announces interest rate decisions that move global gold prices by hundreds of rupees per gram within hours. Yet most Indian gold sellers have no idea why this happens.

Understanding the Fed-gold relationship lets you anticipate major gold price movements - and time significant gold sales more intelligently.

At a Glance

Why does the US Fed affect Indian gold?

Gold is priced globally in USD; Fed rate decisions move the USD and therefore INR gold price

Fed rate hike effect on gold

Usually negative - gold tends to fall when rates rise

Fed rate cut effect on gold

Usually positive - gold tends to rise when rates are cut

How large are the moves?

$10–$50/oz per Fed decision, translating to ₹100–₹600/10g in India

When are Fed meetings?

~8 times per year; schedule at federalreserve.gov

Last Updated

May 2026

How to Use Fed Calendars for Gold Timing

  • Find the Fed meeting schedule: federalreserve.gov publishes FOMC meeting dates for the year
  • Note the 'market expectation': CME FedWatch tool shows what the market expects from the meeting
  • If market expects a cut and Fed delivers: muted reaction (already priced in)
  • If market expects no change but Fed cuts: gold rises sharply (surprise positive)
  • If Fed is more hawkish than expected: gold falls more than anticipated
  • For Indian sellers: the 2–3 days around FOMC meetings are often the most volatile gold rate periods

The USD/INR Amplifier

Fed rate hikes also typically strengthen the US dollar. A stronger dollar means the rupee weakens. Since gold is priced in USD:
• Fed raises rates → USD strengthens → rupee weakens → INR gold price has two pressures: USD gold falls AND rupee weakens
• The net effect on INR gold is complex: sometimes a USD gold fall is offset by rupee weakness

This is why monitoring both the USD gold price AND the USD/INR rate matters for Indian sellers during Fed meeting periods.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does the US Federal Reserve affect India's gold rate?

Yes - significantly. Fed rate decisions move USD gold prices, which combined with USD/INR exchange rate changes, affect the IBJA rate.

What happens to gold when the Fed raises rates?

Gold typically falls in USD terms as higher rates make bonds more attractive. However, if the rupee also weakens, the INR gold impact can be partially offset.

When does the US Federal Reserve meet?

The FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) meets approximately 8 times a year. The schedule is published at federalreserve.gov.

Should I time my gold sale around Fed meetings?

Avoid selling the day before a major Fed decision if you can - the rate can move significantly. If the rate is at a level you're comfortable with, sell regardless of Fed timing.

How much does a Fed rate cut typically move Indian gold?

A 0.25% Fed rate cut can move USD gold by $15–$40/oz, translating to approximately ₹150–₹400 per 10g in India.

Where can I check when the next Fed meeting is?

federalreserve.gov lists all FOMC meeting dates. Financial news sites (CNBC, Bloomberg, Economic Times) also publish this schedule.

Does a Fed rate cut always push gold higher?

Usually yes, but if the cut was already fully expected by markets, gold may not move much. Surprises (more or less than expected) cause the largest moves.

When the branch staff XRF tests your gold, you may see a screen or printout with numbers like 'Au: 91.6%, Ag: 2.1%, Cu: 6.3%'. Do you know what these mean - and how to verify the rate you are being offered reflects the correct reading?

This guide decodes a typical XRF gold testing report so you can verify the result yourself at the branch.

At a Glance

Au on XRF report

Gold (from Latin Aurum) - the percentage you are paid on

Ag on XRF report

Silver (from Latin Argentum) - not paid separately

Cu on XRF report

Copper - not paid separately

Zn

Zinc - not paid separately

Cd

Cadmium - indicates old KDM solder

Au: 91.6%

= 22K gold - standard Indian jewellery

= 18K gold

Reading the Key Number: Au%

The only number you need to verify your payout is the Au% (gold percentage).

How to verify:
1. Note the Au% shown: e.g. Au: 91.6%
2. Divide by 100 to get the purity fraction: 0.916
3. Multiply by the IBJA 24K rate (₹15,250/g): 0.916 × ₹15,250 = ₹13,965/g
4. Multiply by your piece's weight: e.g. 15g × ₹13,965 = ₹2,09,535
5. The buyer's offer should be within 1–3% of this number

If the offer is more than 3% below this calculated figure - ask why.

What to Do If the XRF Reading Seems Wrong

  • Ask for the test to be repeated at a different spot on the piece
  • Ask to see the probe placement - make sure it is on the main gold body, not a solder join
  • For pieces with multiple components (pendant + chain), each may be tested separately
  • You can request a printed copy of the XRF result
  • If still unsatisfied, bring the piece to a second buyer or certified assay centre

Frequently Asked Questions

What does Au 91.6% mean on an XRF report?

Au stands for gold (Aurum). 91.6% gold = 22 karat gold (916 hallmark) - the standard Indian jewellery purity.

What does Ag mean on an XRF gold test?

Ag stands for silver (Argentum). It is an alloy component in gold jewellery - not paid separately. Its presence does not reduce your gold rate.

What does Cd on an XRF result mean?

Cd is cadmium - a sign of old KDM solder. It does not increase your payout and may contribute to a lower overall Au% reading.

How do I calculate my payout from the XRF reading?

Payout = Au% ÷ 100 × IBJA 24K rate (₹15,250/g) × weight (g). Example: Au 91.6%, 10g = 0.916 × ₹15,250 × 10 = ₹1,39,690.

Can the XRF machine be manipulated to give a wrong reading?

Calibrated commercial XRF machines are very difficult to manipulate. If you suspect an issue, ask for a re-test or visit a second buyer.

What if my gold shows Au 89%? What rate do I get?

You receive the rate for 89% gold - between the 22K and 21K rates. Approximately {inr(round(0.890*R24))}/g.

Should I ask for a printout of the XRF result?

Yes - you can request this. It serves as documentation of the tested purity for your records.

html:
You have seen it on YouTube: rub gold on white paper, pour bleach on it, test with a magnet. Dozens of home methods claim to tell you if gold is real.

But how accurate are these tests? Which ones have some scientific basis? And which are complete myths that give false confidence - or false alarm?

Here is the honest science on every common home gold test.

At a Glance

Only definitive test

XRF testing - at a certified branch

Most reliable home test

Acid test (if you have access to 18K testing acid)

Useless for purity

Toothpaste, vinegar, water float, lip/bite test

Can detect fakes

Magnet test (can rule out steel-based fakes)

Can rule out gold plating?

Acid test (partially) - but destroys surface

Last Updated

May 2026

Home Gold Test Methods - Accuracy Rated

Test

What It Claims to Do

Accuracy

Scientific Basis

Magnet test

Gold is not magnetic - magnets won't stick

Partial

Valid for ruling out iron/steel fakes - but gold-plated steel fails too; real gold passes

Toothpaste rub

Rubbing toothpaste on gold - changes colour = fake

No basis

No scientific basis - toothpaste reacts with many metals unpredictably; unreliable

White vinegar

Gold won't change colour; fake gold may discolour

Weak

Gold is acid-resistant - dilute acetic acid (vinegar) may affect very low-karat base metals; fails on gold-plated items

Bleach / chlorine

Real gold doesn't react; fake does

Partial

Gold resists bleach; but bleach can damage both real and fake gold; unsafe

Nitric acid test

18K acid causes reaction on <18K; no reaction on >18K

Moderate

Has a real basis - professional acid test with graded acids; NOT vinegar

Float test

Real gold sinks; fake gold floats

No basis

Gold does sink - but so does many heavy fake metals like tungsten. Doesn't distinguish.

Skin test (discolouration)

Gold shouldn't discolour skin

Partial

Very high-copper alloys (low karat) can discolour skin - but gold-plated base metals also do this

XRF testing

Identifies exact gold % and all elements

Highly accurate

X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy - industry standard

The Only Tests with Real Basis

  • Magnet test: genuine gold is non-magnetic. If your piece sticks to a magnet, it is definitely not solid gold. However, passing the magnet test does not confirm it is gold - many metals (copper, aluminium, stainless steel, tungsten) are also non-magnetic.
  • Acid test (professional): a series of graded nitric acid solutions (8K, 10K, 14K, 18K, 22K) applied to a tiny scratch on the piece. Each acid reacts differently depending on gold content. This is the basis of professional acid testing - but household vinegar is too weak to be meaningful.
  • Hallmark check: looking for the BIS stamp (916, 750, 585) with magnifying glass. Not a test per se - but the quickest first check for Indian jewellery.

Why XRF Is Still the Only Reliable Method

Home tests can only give partial answers - they confirm or deny specific narrow things (magnetic or not) without telling you the actual gold percentage. A gold-plated tungsten bar passes the magnet test and the float test. A 9K gold piece passes vinegar and magnet but is only 37.5% gold.

XRF testing identifies the precise percentage of gold, silver, copper, palladium and every other element in the piece - without scratching or damaging it. It is the only test that gives you a number you can plug into a calculation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does the toothpaste test for gold work?

No - there is no scientific basis for the toothpaste gold test. Toothpaste reacts unpredictably with many metals.

Does white vinegar test for real gold?

Dilute acetic acid (vinegar) is far too weak to accurately test gold. It may react with very low-karat alloys but does not give reliable results for jewellery-grade gold.

Does the magnet test work for gold?

Partially - gold is non-magnetic, so if a piece sticks to a magnet it is definitely not solid gold. However, many fake metals are also non-magnetic, so passing the test doesn't confirm it is gold.

How do I test gold purity at home without equipment?

What is the most accurate way to test gold?

XRF (X-ray fluorescence) testing at a certified branch - the industry standard method that identifies the exact gold content without damaging the piece.

Is free XRF testing available?

Can bleach damage real gold?

Yes - chlorine bleach can degrade gold alloys, particularly those with silver or copper. Avoid using bleach to test gold.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is kacha gold?

Kacha gold (raw/impure) refers to gold of uncertain or mixed purity - typically old, unverified pieces. Pakka gold (pure/verified) refers to hallmarked, tested gold. The terms are used informally by buyers and sellers in markets across India.

Does kacha gold pay less?

Yes - kacha gold (unknown purity) is XRF tested at the branch. If it tests at a lower purity than expected, you receive less per gram. Pakka (hallmarked) gold typically tests at its stated purity.

How do I convert kacha gold to pakka?

Have it XRF tested at a certified branch. If the purity is confirmed and the piece is hallmarked, it is effectively pakka. Older pieces without hallmarks are considered kacha until tested.

Is kacha gold worth less money?

Per gram, no - if it tests at 22K, it receives the 22K rate. But kacha gold is riskier because the purity is unverified until tested.

Where does this terminology come from?

Kacha-pakka (raw-cooked / impure-pure) is a broad Hindi/Urdu concept applied to many materials. In gold markets, it specifically refers to the verification status of purity.

Does kacha gold come from specific sources?

Often from inheritance, old jewellery collections, or pieces bought from informal sources before mandatory hallmarking.
